heard: This man sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap metal. Paris, 1925. Victor Lustig is reading the paper when he spots a tiny story. The tower is rusting and repainting it costs a fortune. So he forges government letterhead and becomes a deputy director at the Ministry of Posts. He books a suite at the hotel de Creon and invites five scrap dealers. His pitch, the city, is secretly tearing the tower down. 7,000 tons of iron. One dealer, Andre P. de Vissone wants it badly, but something feels off. So Lustig makes a confession. He's a corrupt official and he needs a bribe. You see, to P. W. Assone, the bribe was the proof. Only a real official would ask for one. So PWAsone pays $20,000 plus $50,000 more to win. Within the hour, Lustig is on a train to Vienna with the cash. He waits for the headlines. Nothing. PWAsone is too embarrassed to report it. So Lustig comes back to Paris and tries to sell the tower again. This time, the buyer calls the police and Lustig escapes to America. But historians have never found a single police report. The only proof might be a con man's word.
